newsitem.title: MALI: Mali's top court blocks new electoral code.
newsitem.headline: Mali's top court blocks new electoral code.

text.p: Mali's constitutional court has blocked the West African nation's new electoral code, which was passed by parliament but provoked a serious rift with the opposition, court sources said on Monday.
The court ruled that 30 of the new law's 196 articles, including those relating to the composition of the independent electoral commission, were totally or partly unconstitutional, the sources added.

Mali holds presidential, legislative and municipal elections early in 1997. The elections will be the first test of its fledgling democracy, introduced as in many Francophone countries in Africa in the early 1990s.
President Alpha Omar Konare and his government, which enjoys a majority in the national assembly, pushed the new code through parliament on September 27.
The opposition, denouncing a lack of dialogue, took part in neither the debates nor the vote. It asked the court to review the code in light of its objections.
The court has made no public statement on its ruling, delivered on Friday. The government has yet to react.

Konare, a historian, was elected president during Mali's successful democratic transition in 1992. The Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA), which backs him, won 76 of the assembly's 116 seats. It now holds 70.

The opposition, previously fragmented but starting to work together in fragile alliances, says the proposed electoral commission -- five members each for the ruling party and the opposition plus 10 each for society at large and the public authorities -- would not be independent.
It has also described the proposed method of polling -- a mix of proportional representation in some areas and a majority vote in others -- as confusing and unfair.
